title: mTLS Identity Propagation in Go Microservices: Certificate Chains, SPIFFE SVIDs, and the Trust Boundary Collapse Problem
description: How mTLS peer identity travels across Go service hops, where trust boundaries silently collapse, and what you must enforce at each layer.
linkedin_post:
Most teams treat mTLS as the finish line for service-to-service security. It isn't.

mTLS proves identity across one hop. In a three-service chain — gateway → order-service → inventory-service — inventory-service sees order-service's SPIFFE SVID. It sees nothing about the gateway or the originating request. If order-service is compromised, it can drive inventory-service freely using its own legitimate certificate.

This is the trust boundary collapse problem. SVID-level RBAC is necessary but not sufficient when a single compromised service has ambient write authority over downstream systems.

My latest article goes deep on the production mechanics:

→ How SPIFFE SVIDs propagate (and where the propagation gap lives)
→ Caller-chain attestation: signing SVID chains so downstream services can verify the full originating path
→ Why you must verify the chain header at every hop, not just the first
→ Certificate rotation and connection pool invalidation in Go — why your http.Transport will hold stale peer identities after SVID expiry
→ Trust domain federation across AWS accounts and the over-federation failure mode
→ A practical decision framework for when each layer of enforcement is warranted

The Go examples cover peer SVID extraction from TLS state, chain signing with the workload's own key, and SVID-aware connection pool logic that prevents stale identity from persisting across certificate rotation.

If you're running a Go microservice mesh and you haven't thought about what happens after the TLS handshake, this is worth reading.
